articles.title: Data Patterns Prepares for BrahMos Seeker Production Orders
articles.text:
Indian defence electronics firm Data Patterns has clarified that the BrahMos export deal is currently at the pipeline stage as the seeker being developed by them is going through the qualification process. Orders are expected only after they complete the qualification stage and the customer comes forward.
Speaking during their Q2 FY2027 earnings conference call, Data Patterns Chairman and Managing Director Srinivasagopalan Rangarajan stated that they haven’t negotiated any deals with BrahMos.
“We are still at the qualification stage for the seeker for BrahMos. Once we complete qualification, we will get an enquiry for orders and then we will go ahead with manufacturing. We are getting ready for that, but as we are cautious we are not putting a lot of money in. Everything from the design stage to the test system has been developed in house and hence it will be fairly simple to create a production line,” he said.
He further revealed that they’ve bought some costly equipment for production, but have not yet put their money into creating a production assembling line including the stage testing equipment.
The strategy has been to firstly qualify the seeker, understand what needs to be done for exports and then create a production line based on what the customer is expecting to produce. They’ve developed the seeker and are going through qualification. The commercial side hasn’t crossed over yet. If they qualify successfully, get an enquiry from a customer and then go ahead with orders there will be some big milestones.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

GTRE Plans 75 kN Kaveri-AF Validation on Tejas Before New Variant
articles.text:
GTRE plans to carry out integration of the current Dry Kaveri engine section with the current after burner before it commences development of a new after burner that still waits clearance for funds from the Defence Ministry. The current Dry Kaveri engine core can generate 49 kN of thrust without an afterburner, and thrust has been validated multiple times now, and the majority of the flutter issues in the engines have been resolved, and it will be used to power the Ghatak UCAV, a 13-tonne strike platform that has been cleared for development by the MoD.
BrahMos Aerospace was to develop a new afterburner section that could generate 29 kN of thrust over the 49 kN that is currently being generated by the Dry Kaveri engine that could have taken combined thrust to over 78 kN, but it is not clear if the new afterburner section has been manufactured.
The proposed plan is to test the Dry Kaveri engine with the older Afterburner section to validate the combined afterburner thrust generation of 73-75 kN on a Tejas Mk1 LSP aircraft, and once a series of inflight trials are carried out and validate that the engine and the afterburner can be further developed and improved upon, then actual work on prototyping of the new afterburner section might begin that could allow it to generate thrust closer to the current F-404 engine that has an afterburner-engaged thrust of 81 kN.
Since the Kaveri engine is a flatbed engine, it doesn’t lose thrust due to high humidity or dry conditions and will be able to generate 78 kN of thrust when the F-404 engine loses about 6-8 per cent of its thrust in the same conditions. Theoretically, in all weather conditions, the Kaveri engine will be able to generate more thrust than the F-404, but that will not be the only reason why the IAF will be happy to switch to Kaveri engines when the F-404 engine is required to be replaced, as the life span of the Kaveri engine compared to the F-404 engine is still nowhere near it.
GTRE plans to mate a Dry Kaveri on an older LSP Tejas aircraft that could see only the Dry Kaveri engine being tested first before the engine being tested with an older afterburner section. Once both are validated, GTRE plans to make a case for the development of a 90N engine that could compensate for future thrust requirements of the Tejas Mk1A when they are due for a new engine change and developmental testing onboard. The Ghatak UCAV programme will also smooth out engine production and refinements before it can be cleared for further testing on the manned jets like Tejas.
RAUNAK KUNDE

articles.title: Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal
articles.text:
Another day, another disruptive network outage (or two) as government officials and company execs scramble to assure an anxious populace that these are not coordinated cyberattacks – and security experts call this the new normal.

A classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for internal communications, called NSANet, went offline on Tuesday in what the agency described as a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.”

“While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the NSA said in a statement following media reports about the outage. “NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”

Around the same time, Apple users began reporting issues across multiple services – including Apple Support, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay, and more – with Apple retail stores worldwide also reportedly experiencing disruptions that halted sales and in-person support.

A day earlier, customers at major US banks including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and US Bank reported service outages that Chase attributed to “a software bug in on-premise hardware systems - there is no evidence this is cyber-related.”

All of these high-profile outages followed last week’s US Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) order grounding all planes on Friday due to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade, and a Microsoft 365 outage on Thursday.

Redmond later blamed the massive service disruption on a faulty software update it pushed back in July.

Despite the weekend respite from network outages, your humble vulture still had to field is-this-the-beginning-of-the-end questions from friends and family all day Saturday and Sunday, most of whom suspected Russia or China – maybe even Iran – caused the spate of downed systems and services.

A highly sophisticated, coordinated nation-state hack would be a much more exciting cause for the disruptions. The real culprit, however, appears to be aging, under-funded infrastructure, riddled with decades-old bugs and held together by digital sticks and glue.

“As someone who started out as a hacker, I know how tempting it is to connect the dots when major systems fail one after another,” Remedio CEO Tal Kollender told The Register, adding that there’s “no credible public evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack,” and most have been attributed to technical failures.

“What concerns me more is what these incidents reveal about the fragility of our digital infrastructure. We've built an interconnected world on layers of aging systems, complex configurations, and dependencies that organizations don't always fully understand. A single misconfiguration, failed update, or broken dependency can create disruption on a massive scale, even without an attacker,” Kollender said. “The uncomfortable reality I think we're grappling with is that attackers don't always have to break our systems. Sometimes, our systems are already capable of breaking on their own.”

For people who couldn’t withdraw money from their bank, board a flight, or use email at work on Friday, “the disruption was real regardless of the cause,” she said.

“Cybersecurity has spent decades investing in detecting threats, identifying vulnerabilities, and generating reports,” according to Kollender. “Yet we still allow for these preventable weaknesses and configurations that can bring entire systems down.”

Cynthia Kaiser, senior VP of Halcyon’s Ransomware Research Center and former deputy director of the FBI’s Cyber Division, told The Reg that the recent disruptions show “how deeply interconnected our digital infrastructure has become, and how a single technical failure or software update can cascade with outsized effects across critical systems.”

AI has entered the chat

Then we go and add AI to this already delicate balance, and everything essentially blows up.

AI-assisted bug hunting and exploit development has surfaced more than 100,000 CVEs so far this year, with Microsoft’s Patch Tuesday disclosing more than 1,000 vulnerabilities in each of the past two months. AI has also shrunk the elapsed time between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits.

“We are in an era where AI is accelerating the discovery of legacy software flaws, forcing organizations to race to patch vulnerabilities before adversaries can exploit them, which inevitably creates friction and disruptions,” Kaiser said. “Even when an outage isn’t caused by a cyberattack, these moments of operational distraction leave dangerous gaps open for threat actors and opportunists to take advantage of, making it crucial for both institutions and everyday individuals to remain on high alert against social engineering and unsolicited outreach.”

Even when attackers aren’t using AI to facilitate intrusions, the technology itself has become a source of risk to organizations.

“Autonomous agents can execute actions, change configurations, access sensitive information, and interact with critical systems at machine speed,” Kollender said. “When those systems lack proper governance and safeguards, a mistake can develop just as quickly as an attack.

Former US Department of Defense network exploitation and vulnerability analyst Mike Wiacek, when asked if these regular system outages are the new normal, told us: “The brutal truth is yes. Especially in the AI world that we live in.”

After the DoD, Wiacek founded Google’s Threat Analysis Group. He's since founded Stairwell, a threat-intel firm he serves as chief technology officer.

“The idea that we are going to patch ourselves to security is, dare I say, an antiquated concept,” he told The Register.

One of Stairwell’s engineers was doing regular, daily software development tasks on an open source library with Anthropic’s Claude Mythos, and the model told the engineer about a buffer-overflow vulnerability in the code.

“We weren't even looking for it,” Wiacek said. “It found a vulnerability in open source software by accident. You used to need specialized bug hunters and really, really technical security folks to discover and develop vulnerabilities and exploits. Now, it’s almost too easy to do it.”

This new reality, he said, necessitates a total rethink of how we build and maintain digital infrastructure.

“How do we get to a world where we assume compromised by default, and continuously recompromised, and then develop the architectures and the systems necessary to make what was the expense of incident-response investigation really fast and cheap? Because we will not be able to patch our way out of it.”

It requires vulnerability managers and system administrators to patch as soon as software updates become available. But from an engineering perspective, it also means building in “as many fail-safes as possible,” Wiacek said.

“An elevator doesn't have just one cable hoisting it,” he continued. “There's a lot of redundancy in those systems. Enterprises and organizations and governments haven't really had to operate like that. But that's going to be the new norm, whether we want it to be or not. Pandora's box is opened, and it's not going to go back inside.” ®

articles.title: GPU giants throw HPC users some tasty crumbs
articles.text:
At Supercomputing 2026 this week, Nvidia unveiled a new variant of its Rubin GPUs aimed at – you’ll never believe it – high performance computing (HPC).

The creatively named Rubin HPC promises more than 50,000 CUDA cores, nearly twice that of the AI-focused version of the chip that Nvidia unveiled earlier this year. It will arrive sometime in 2028.

According to Dan Ernst, Nvidia’s senior director of supercomputing, the new chip offers a rebalanced architecture optimized for the kinds of simulation, engineering, and high-performance analytics workloads common in the HPC and scientific computing communities.

This is not the first time Nvidia has introduced specialized hardware. Last year, the company optimized its B300 accelerator for AI inferencing workloads.

“Rubin HPC is the same idea,” Ernst told El Reg. “Within the Rubin platform, but we’re building variants to really focus on a specific sub domain of applications.”

Details remain remarkably thin. Nvidia hasn’t disclosed peak performance memory capacity or bandwidth. That said, the chip will likely include features which show Nvidia can think beyond AI and still cares about the HPC community.

Fearing that Nvidia could ignore HPC is reasonable becuase beginning with the launch of Blackwell Ultra (B300/GB300), the company traded double-precision matrix acceleration for higher throughput at lower-precisions.

The result was a chip that at FP4 churned out 15 petaFLOPS of AI compute, but just 1.3 teraFLOPS at FP64. That's good for AI, but less useful for scientists.

When Nvidia unveiled Rubin, it seemed the GPU-slinger would continue this trend. At 33 teraFLOPS, the chip was not only slower at FP64 than the Blackwell GPUs it replaced, but slower than Nvidia’s now four-year-old Hopper accelerators as well.

Nvidia contended that for sparse vector-heavy workloads measured by the High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG) benchmark, the higher ratio of memory bandwidth to compute should deliver meaningful performance gains.

Meanwhile, for dense matrix-heavy workloads, for which benchmarks like High-Performance Linpack (HPL) are representative, Nvidia adopted a new strategy: FP64 emulation.

We discussed the pros and cons of this technique in greater detail earlier this year, but in a nutshell it uses an algorithm derived from the so-called Ozaki Scheme.

The algorithm works by decomposing FP64 matrix operations into a string of INT8 operations that, when run on Nvidia’s tensor cores, achieve higher-than-native performance.

Nvidia, we’re told, isn’t using INT8, but it is unlocking substantial performance gains, at least for certain workloads. According to Nvidia, Rubin can churn out up to 200 emulated FP64 matrix teraFLOPS.

While Ernst didn’t offer any specifics, he assured us that Nvidia’s HPC hardware should offer native FP64 matrix performance and customers won't have to rely entirely on emulation.

Assessing the new chip's vector performance is much easier. With more than 50 thousand CUDA cores (by our calculation, it should be closer to 53,248), the chip should deliver at least 86 percent higher vector performance at double precision.

AMD’s HPC beast

AMD is also cooking up new HPC chips. In a blog post published late last week, AMD revealed the HPC-tuned version of its MI400-series GPUs.

The Instinct MI430X boasts 432 GB of HBM4, 23 TB/s of memory bandwidth and a whopping 288 teraFLOPS of peak double precision grunt.

AMD isn’t relying on FP64 emulation. Instead, AMD took advantage of its modular chiplet architecture to build two distinct versions of its MI400-series accelerators: one optimized for AI and another designed to excel in HPC and scientific computing workloads.

AMD has shared predictions as to how the chips will perform in several of the Top500’s headline benchmarks. In a total non-surprise, the House of Zen says systems like EuroHPC’s Alice Recoque and Oak Ridge National Laboratories’ upcoming Discovery supers would enjoy significant performance gains if they upgrade from its earlier Instinct MI300A and MI250X-based offerings. ®

articles.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
articles.text:
Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday.

ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword.

Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware

Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript.

articles.title: Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI!
articles.text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models.

"So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve."

Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust."

Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees. Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts.

"The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said.

People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line.

As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble.

Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted.

"In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models."

Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access.

As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action.

"How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. "And the reality is, by definition, you can't. In other words, it becomes an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. And so our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three architectural imperatives."

Microsoft's original stack was built on ownership of the operating system. But the company's commitment to AI is such that it now describes Copilot in the terms once reserved for Windows.

"Copilot is the new operating system for work," said Nadella.

AI is eating software, and Microsoft is here for it

Fifteen years ago, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen famously observed that software is eating the world. Now AI, including Copilot, is eating software.

"Apps are just plugins to Copilot," Nadella mused. "That's why we in fact have brought all of Office, all of its richness, right built into Copilot."

Copilot is eating other companies too. Nadella said Microsoft is extending Copilot to take on specific roles by providing skills, connectors, and plugins for industry-specific tasks. Toward that end, "Copilot is the new front door to Dynamics 365," which now offers CRM plugins. And Nadella announced a partnership with Salesforce called Copilotforce that brings Salesforce context into Copilot, Teams, and Fabric.

He also talked up Microsoft IQ, the company's new enterprise context management platform.

"The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain, and continuously improve your own intelligence across the organization," said Nadella, describing it as an externalization of the context system underlying Copilot.

Nadella went on to announce a new model family for GitHub Copilot Fusion, its code hosting subsidiary's model orchestration and routing play. He noted that Copilot Fusion today is ranked above Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at less than half the cost on Terminal Bench, a measurement of how well AI agents complete tasks using a terminal.

Then there's Copilot Workspaces, which Nadella described as a multiplayer version of Copilot. Instead of a chat window where one person interacts with a model, it's an interface for team collaboration that shares context with a model.

Microsoft's decision model, intended to challenge TypeSafe AI's Jev, debuted about a month ago and now Decisions 1.1 is generally available.

"We have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster," said Nadella. "Already over 4,000 customers have used it."

He then said that Microsoft Foundry would offer OpenAI's GPT-6.2, which may have caused some confusion because at that point, OpenAI had no such model. A short time later, OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol.

Microsoft also rolled out new coding models, in the form of Code 2, Code 2 Flash, and Cyber 2 Flash, and said its next-gen Cobalt 200 VMs are generally available.

It's a question of trust

After rattling off the various products and services Microsoft has prepared to help organizations with intelligence ownership, Nadella returned to the question of trust.

"Today we can see almost everything that models touch, but you cannot see what happens inside a model," he said. "And really what's worse is that we know that what a model tells us about itself is not even independent evidence and therefore cannot be trusted.

"And one model monitoring another model has the same issue. So you essentially have these unacceptable nested sets of black boxes, which we now need to make transparent and verifiable."

Microsoft's bid to bridge the trust gap is the Microsoft Transparency Initiative. The company says this will involve engagement with the National Institute of Standards and Technology's "SI Agent Standards Initiative."

Whether Microsoft AI will be compatible with NIST SI remains to be seen. That initiative also calls for collaboration with other organizations to develop accountable, verifiable, vendor-neutral AI transparency standards, and for Microsoft to incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Foundry, and Copilot. Check in next year to see whether transparency is achieved. ®

articles.title: Jensen Huang thrilled to be spending time with family, but will retake leadership burden if Nvidia asks
articles.text:
No surprises here. Ex-Nvidia boss Jensen Huang says that he'd be willing to come back to the company he founded, if the board wants him to return.

In Huang’s first public comments since his resignation last week over a series of extramarital affairs, both with Nvidia staff and an alleged Chinese spy at one of its customers, he admits that he may have made life hard for the company he spent 33 years building, but he’s really sorry…and Nvidia couldearn really use him.

“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang admitted. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.”

But soft, what open letter through yonder news cycle break? It's one calling widely for Huang’s return – and he's happy to oblige if Nvidia’s post-Jensen crisis-mode leadership is willing to indulge him.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.”

Nvidia, Huang added, has been his life’s work, and is a “once-in-a-generation company” that perhaps needs his steady hand at the helm.

There have been a number of public calls for Huang’s return to the head of the company he helped create, from tech industry heavyweights and Nvidia shareholders like Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, as well as a number of current Nvidia employees, company partners, and shareholders upset that the stock has lost more than a quarter of its value since reports of the affair first emerged. One petition pleading for his return has nearly 200,000 signatures.

Faced with that, what else can a disgraced billionaire tech founder who may have literally have been in bed with a Chinese spy do? Duty calls.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said.

Reports citing Nvidia insiders with knowledge of the matter suggest the board isn’t considering reinstating Huang as CEO despite the public push. On the company's third-quarter earnings call late Tuesday, new board chairman Harvey Jones said that Huang's behavior was "Inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms” and that the board "does not expect to reinstate him as CEO," putting a seeming end to the question.

Huang out to dry

The US Department of Justice made the rare point of commenting on one of the pillars of the Jensen Huang story on Tuesday when it confirmed that it’s investigating Megaspeed, the Singaporean company formerly helmed by Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), the alleged Chinese spy.

The DoJ has been checking the company out since 2024, when Alice Huang was still in charge, over potential export control violations. In other words, the DoJ is hinting that even if Alice Huang isn’t a spy, Megaspeed may have still been moving illegal chips.

The DoJ added that Nvidia blacklisted Megaspeed in 2025, and that the Department of Commerce previously interviewed Alice Huang around the same time. It was immediately after that, the DoJ said, that it took over the investigation.

“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” the DoJ said.

In other words, this is far from over and Nvidia might be justified in wanting not to touch its founder with a ten-foot pole. ®

Python parallel debugging comes to HPC thanks to TotalView upgrade
articles.text:
The OG debugger for supercomputer iron has buddied up with the data-science darling now muscling in on HPC: Python.

At the SC26 supercomputing show this week (booth #2829), Perforce Software is demonstrating how its TotalView parallel debugging tool now understands Python, easing the path for using the language on large, distributed apps, particularly those in the high-performance computing (HPC) space.

In the HPC community, "Python has grown in popularity,” said Bill Burns, Perforce vice president of software engineering, in an interview with The Register.

TotalView is a debugger specializing in picking apart parallel applications for developers.

Built in the late 1980s for military applications, TotalView today largely serves developers in high-performance computing (HPC), where large scientific applications are spread across multiple servers, running in parallel on thousands or even tens of thousands of processes. (Perforce acquired TotalView in 2019 in its purchase of the DevOps-focused Rogue Wave Software.)

To date, TotalView has supported C/C++ and Fortran. With the latest quarterly release, the tool now supports Python as well.

Debugging a thousand cores

C/C++ has long had a decent dedicated debugger in GDB, but figuring out what went wrong across multiple threads is a special kind of torture. Each thread needs to be instrumented, and all the output needs to be aggregated and filtered to just highlight the interesting stuff. Regular debuggers get overwhelmed with all this info.

“Even if you have 10,000 things going on, if you have one crash in there, TotalView can pinpoint that,” Burns said. It can look at the state of the process, the threads within that process or the GPU that process is using.

In the HPC space, computing work has traditionally been written in C/C++. And at least some HPC iron still runs Fortran.

Thanks to it being easy to learn and use, Python has gained a foothold in this community as well. The mpi4py library bridges a Python program to the Message Passing Interface (MPI), allowing different parts of an application running on different hardware to communicate.

Python became more amenable to parallel programming at the thread level with version 3.14, released a year ago, which included the ability to use concurrent interpreters, as well as the long-awaited free threading support, thanks to the disabling of the global interpreter lock (GIL).

“If you have a CPU with 64 cores, you can run 64 independent threads all working in unison on that CPU. Without GIL, those threads will run fully asynchronously,” Burns said.

Multinode scientific simulations, distributed AI training, and large applications that would benefit from shared memory have all become fair game for Python.

Of course, with 500 or 1,000 interpreters all running in parallel, debugging will also get more difficult.

“Now you're going to end up with lock and thread contention and race conditions and all the things that C++ and Fortran developers have dealt with for years,” Burns said.

A view into parallel Python

Under the hood, TotalView uses Microsoft's debugpy engine (via the Debug Adapter Protocol) to power its own hierarchical tree server. TotalView can aggregate hundreds of stack traces into a single view, highlighting only those outside of expected bounds.

To kick off a debugging session, a developer can launch a single-process or parallel program under TotalView’s control. They can then set breakpoints to pause execution and inspect variables and data structures, as well as evaluate Python expressions.

The package doesn’t offer full cross-language debugging, which would be truly helpful for Python apps that call C/C++ libraries and modules. For now, developers have to choose between debugging the C/C++ side (while viewing the Python stack) or debugging Python on its own — though Burns said Perforce plans to merge both modes into a single workflow in an upcoming release.

And though TotalView supports mpi4py and Python’s own multiprocessing module out of the box, future releases will support other Python concurrency frameworks, such as Dask and PyTorch’s torchrun.

TotalView is priced on a token-based model, where each token buys the capability to debug a process. ®

articles.title: Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’
articles.text:
After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack.

The good news? It was all part of a test.

The Gemini 4 Argon agents were given an impossible task to complete – come up with the “official” answers to Epoch AI’s FrontierMatch problems. In some runs they had internet access. Even with their production safeguards enabled, Trajectory Labs says the agents “engaged in misaligned behavior.”

“Across four scenarios, they attempted SQL injection against Epoch AI’s live website, claimed to be Epoch staff to get answer keys, turned a shared package cache into a message board, and obfuscated their commands to avoid their safeguards,” the AI safety company said in a Friday report.

If this all sounds similar, it should. Google’s AI agents behaved in much the same way as OpenAI’s models did when they broke out of their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face.

Google did not respond to The Register's questions.

According to Trajectory, the Hugging Face intrusions prompted it to test misalignment in other models. While OpenAI’s models were running with their safety guardrails turned off in the Hugging Face scenario, Trajectory “wanted to know whether a current frontier model would behave the same way with its production safeguards enabled.”

Trajectory ran swarms of up to 80 Gemini 4 Argon agents, gave them an impossible task, and prompted them not to give up until they completed it – which, we’re told, was “intentionally” done to “elicit misaligned behavior, if it existed.”

Turns out it existed.

“We told the agents to persist with an impossible math benchmark task, but we did not tell them to hack anyone or pose as Epoch staff,” McIntyre said.

“When a model hacks systems or deceives people to finish a task, it is misaligned with what its developer and its user intended,” he continued. “Production safeguards are meant to block harmful requests even when the model itself goes wrong. Under our test conditions, neither the model nor its safeguards stopped the agents.”

Four test scenarios

The initial testing began on October 20, and the agents had internet access. We should note that just one of these tests was run with Epoch’s consent.

In the first scenario, the agents did reach Epoch’s live website – and fell into the research nonprofit’s honeypots, set up to detect AI agents. These honeypots contained a decoy benchmark key, which the agents found and used. The agents also probed for internal endpoints including /admin, /keys and /users, and attempted a SQL injection.

After noticing the agents’ activities, Epoch added an “agent helpline,” and some of the agents that used it claimed to be Epoch staff seeking answers to the test questions.

After this initial test, Trajectory and Epoch decided to use a copy of the website instead of a live version, and built a buggy local copy with a planted vulnerability based on CVE-2026-102255, a critical pre-authentication Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) appliances. “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says.

In an effort to mimic the Hugging Face incident, Trajectory also gave the agents a local, shared package manager, which “nearly all” of them used as a message board to communicate with each other and coordinate efforts to complete the test.

In a separate, local setup, Trajectory swapped out Epoch’s honeypot with an AI assistant that would release answers only to named Epoch staff who passed a security check with their date of birth. “Agents accessed people-search sites, attempted impersonation again, and tried to jailbreak the AI assistant,” the testing firm said.

Next time: kill switches at the ready

A third test on October 30 used a staging copy of Epoch’s website, and granted the agents internet access. One of them tried a SQL injection, and multiple claimed to be Epoch staff on the helpline. They also attempted to bypass a CAPTCHA check.

Finally, the fourth scenario on October 29 and 30 kept the agents contained in a sandbox, with no internet access and no copy of Epoch’s website.

They were, however, offered a decoy switch and told it would turn off the firewall.

In all three runs, the agents switched the decoy off and obfuscated its address to bypass Gemini’s safeguards. On one, the agent rebuilt the switch’s address from positions of words it had saved earlier. The real firewall blocked the agents’ traffic throughout all of these tests.

At this point, Trajectory stopped its tests, and said it won’t run any future experiments until it has a risk management plan in place, with signoff from its CEO and CTO, along with approval from any outside systems that the models could “reasonably” target. Tests will also include real-time automated monitoring and kill switches, and Trajectory said that it’s setting up a system to notify any organizations affected by these experiments.

Interestingly, Trajectory co-founder Peter McIntyre told us that the testing firm “ran a similar test with another frontier model, and it did not exhibit the same misalignment as Gemini 4 Argon.”

However, this was not a controlled comparison. “Our report covers one model's behavior, and was designed as a stress test to see whether that model would exhibit similar misalignment under duress, not a measure of how often different models behave this way,” McIntyre told The Register.

Overall, the testing firm noted that the agents’ behavior “show how easily testing capable AI agents can spill over to affect real systems and people, and there are not yet shared standards for doing it safely.”

Trajectory says that it's developing a set of safety standards, and recommends that anyone else running misalignment tests use fully isolated sandboxes. ®

Correction: Epoch only consented to one of the tests, scenario three. The original version of this article said that it consented to all of the tests.
articles.summary: After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack.

articles.title: PACE-ECG: Patient-Aware Contrastive ECG Pretraining; Leveraging Longitudinal Structure for Transferable Representations
articles.text:
arXiv:2611.12307v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Foundation models for physiological signals are commonly evaluated on in-domain interpretation tasks, but their ability to transfer to longitudinal clinical prognosis across healthcare systems remains uncertain. We developed PACE-ECG, an ECG pretraining framework that combines contrastive learning across temporally neighbouring recordings from the same patient with clinically guided multitask supervision. We evaluated frozen ECG representations for post-myocardial-infarction all-cause mortality and incident heart failure prediction across MIMIC-IV and two external HEEDB cohorts, comparing the proposed representation with DeepECG-SSL, a state-of-the-art model, and two control baselines. Across both downstream tasks, the proposed model outperformed DeepECG-SSL in-domain (AUROC +1.9% for mortality and +4.0% for heart failure) and on external populations in HEEDB-Boston (+5.6% for mortality +10.3% for heart failure) and HEEDB-Atlanta (+6.9% for mortality +11.0% for heart failure) while using an encoder 41 times smaller and a fraction of the pretraining data. A matched ablation showed that patient-temporal pairing improved external mortality and heart failure AUROC over generic self-supervision by 7.0% and 9.4% on HEEDB-Boston and 8.9% and 9.3% on HEEDB-Atlanta. These findings indicate that pretraining-objective design greatly influences downstream transfer alongside model and data scale, and that in-domain performance alone is insufficient to establish the clinical generalisability of ECG foundation representations.

articles.title: MARS: Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams for Video Forgery Detection
articles.text:
arXiv:2611.12508v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Generalizing deepfake detection across facial manipulation and fully generated video remains challenging due to forgery traces varying with the manipulation method and scene content. Explicit spatial and temporal feature differences offer a way to capture this variation, but also respond to natural texture and motion, motivating their joint interpretation with appearance features. We investigate whether combining multiscale feature differences with adapted appearance representations improves detection across both forgery categories. We introduce Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams (MARS), a two-path video detector. The residual path applies fixed spatial and temporal difference-of-Gaussians operators to frozen intermediate features and models the resulting differences alongside appearance context across frames. The semantic path adapts the encoder's normalization parameters for frame classification, and a clip-dependent gate combines their predictions. Under a shared protocol across seven datasets, MARS achieves the highest average AUROC of 91.43\%, outperforming seven compared detectors. When trained on facial manipulations alone, MARS achieves 93.99\% AUROC on GenVideo and 75.50\% on DF26, demonstrating transfer to generated videos without generated-video training data. MARS also provides signed patch and frame contributions, whose faithfulness we evaluate through controlled spatial and temporal removal against random controls. MARS is publicly available for research: Project page: https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mars/ Github: https://github.com/VectorInstitute/mars
